title: Maximum Element
directAnswer: Back a normal stack with a second 'max stack' that mirrors the running maximum. On push, also push max(newValue, currentMax) onto the max stack. On pop, pop both. The current maximum is always the top of the max stack — O(1) per push, pop, and max query.

remember.pattern: Stack + parallel max-stack tracking the running maximum
remember.formula:
push(x): main.push(x); maxStack.push(max(x, maxStack.peekOrNegInf()))
pop():    main.pop();  maxStack.pop()
getMax(): return maxStack.peek()
rules: Push onto **both** stacks every time; the max stack stores `max(x, previousMax)`, never just `x`.
Pop from **both** stacks together so they stay the same height and stay in sync.
The maximum is always `maxStack.peek()` — never rescan the main stack (that would be O(n)).
When the stack is empty the 'previous max' is −∞ (or just push the first element directly).
Don't try to 'remove the max' on pop by searching — the parallel stack already encodes the max at every depth.
whenToUse: A stack where you must query the max (or min) in O(1) alongside push/pop
Min Stack / Max Stack design questions
Streaming pushes/pops with frequent extreme-value queries
Any LIFO structure needing an O(1) aggregate that's monotone under push/pop
antiSignals: You need the max of a sliding window over a queue → monotonic deque, not a max stack
Arbitrary-position deletes (not just pop) → a stack can't model that; use a heap or balanced BST
You need the k-th largest, not just the max → a heap or order-statistics structure
remember.takeaway: Pair the data stack with a same-height max stack whose top is the running maximum. Push and pop them together and the max is always one peek away. This 'shadow aggregate stack' trick is the standard answer to Min/Max Stack and shows up wherever a LIFO needs an O(1) extreme.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can achieve O(1) max queries by maintaining an auxiliary stack of running maxima, instead of scanning the stack on every query.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recomputing the max by scanning the whole stack on each query (O(n) per query → O(nq) total), or pushing the raw value onto the max stack instead of max(value, previousMax).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the auxiliary-max-stack invariant (its top equals the current maximum), show push/pop keep both stacks the same height, and note this is the same idea as Min Stack.

problemStatement:
You have an empty stack. Process `q` queries, each of one of three types:

- `1 x` — push the integer `x` onto the stack.
- `2` — pop the element on top of the stack.
- `3` — print the **maximum** element currently in the stack.

All type-3 queries must run in O(1). Print the answer to each type-3 query on its own line.
constraints: Type 2 (pop) is only issued when the stack is non-empty
Type 3 (max) is only issued when the stack is non-empty
understanding: Support push, pop, and 'current maximum' on a stack, all in O(1). The maximum can only be affected at the top: pushing may raise it, popping may lower it back to what it was before that element. That history of 'max so far at each depth' is exactly what a parallel stack records.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the max query happen on an empty stack?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the constraints guarantee type-3 (and type-2) queries only occur when the stack is non-empty, so we don't special-case emptiness for them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must each query be O(1), or is O(n) per query acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: O(1) is required. With q up to 10⁵, an O(n) scan per max query risks O(n²) and a timeout.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values repeat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The max stack handles duplicates naturally because it stores the running max, which simply stays the same across equal values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could I store the max only when it changes, to save space?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: You could (an index/count-based variant), but the full parallel stack is simpler and still O(n) space — fine for these limits.

examples.explanation: After the pops, the stack holds [26]; max = 26. Then push 91 → stack [26, 91]; max = 91.
Push 4, push 7 → max 7. Pop 7 → stack [4] → max 4.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Scan the Stack on Every Max Query
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to motivate the optimal, then note the O(n) per query cost violates the O(1) requirement.
hints: Push and pop are trivially O(1) on a stack. The only hard part is the max query.
The simplest max query iterates the whole stack and returns the largest element.
With up to 10⁵ queries and a stack of up to 10⁵ elements, scanning per query is O(n²) — too slow and it ignores the O(1) requirement.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Push/pop are O(1), but each type-3 query scans up to n elements; q such queries give O(q·n) worst case.
approaches.explanation:
Keep a single stack. Push and pop normally. For a max query, walk every element and return the largest.

**Why it's the obvious first cut.** Push and pop are the native stack operations and need nothing extra. The maximum *is* derivable from the contents, so scanning answers it correctly.

**Why it fails the bar.** The problem explicitly wants O(1) max queries. A scan is O(n) per query; with q and n both up to 10⁵ that's up to 10¹⁰ operations and a timeout. It's correct but unacceptably slow — useful only to frame why we precompute the running max.
approaches.insight: The maximum only ever changes at the top of the stack — a push can raise it, a pop can lower it. That locality means we don't need to rescan; we can remember the max at each depth as we build the stack.

approaches.name: Auxiliary Max Stack (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Describe the parallel stack invariant: its top is always the current maximum.
hints: The max changes only at the top. What if, alongside the data, you also stored 'the maximum of everything at or below this position'?
Keep a second stack. On push x, push max(x, currentMax) onto it; on pop, pop it too. Its top is always the current max.
A max query is then just reading the top of the auxiliary stack — O(1), no scan.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each query does a constant number of stack operations → O(1) per query. Two stacks of up to n elements → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain two stacks of equal height: the main stack of values, and a `maxStack` whose top is always the maximum of everything currently in the main stack.

**The invariant.** After every operation, `maxStack.peek()` equals the maximum of the main stack. We preserve it on each operation:

- **Push x:** push `x` onto the main stack and push `max(x, maxStack.peek())` onto `maxStack`. The new running max is either the old max or `x`, whichever is larger. When the stack was empty, the previous max is `−∞`, so we just push `x`.
- **Pop:** pop both stacks. Removing the top value also removes the max-so-far that it introduced, restoring `maxStack`'s top to the maximum of the remaining elements — which is exactly the value that was there before this element was pushed.
- **Max query:** return `maxStack.peek()`.

**Why store `max(x, prevMax)` and not just `x`.** The max stack at depth `d` must answer 'what is the largest value among the bottom `d` elements?'. Storing the running max at each depth makes that a single read. Storing raw values would force a scan, defeating the purpose.

**Why popping both keeps it correct.** The two stacks always have the same height and were filled in lockstep, so the element at depth `d` in `maxStack` corresponds to the prefix of depth `d` in the main stack. Popping both unwinds exactly one push, and the new top of `maxStack` is the max of the new (shorter) prefix.

**Why it's O(1).** Push, pop, and peek on a stack are all constant time, and we do a fixed number of them per query. No scanning, ever.
approaches.insight: The auxiliary stack is a 'shadow aggregate' that records the running maximum at every depth. Because max is monotone as the stack grows, each level's answer is just `max(value, levelBelow)`. The identical pattern with `min` solves Min Stack — recognise it as the canonical way to give a LIFO an O(1) extreme.

Popping only one stack, desynchronising the two heights.
Forgetting the empty-max-stack case on the first push (previous max is −∞).

commonMistakes: Scanning the whole stack on each max query — O(n) per query instead of O(1).
Pushing the raw value onto the max stack rather than max(value, previousMax).
Popping the data stack without popping the max stack, breaking synchronisation.
Mishandling the first push when the max stack is empty.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pushing raw values onto the max stack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The max stack must answer 'max of everything at or below this depth'. Storing the raw value means the top reflects only the latest element, not the running maximum, so the max query is wrong after a smaller value is pushed on top of a larger one.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Popping only one stack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you pop the data stack but not the max stack, the two heights diverge and the max stack's top no longer corresponds to the current contents, corrupting every subsequent max query.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
main.pop()
# forgot max_stack.pop() -> stacks now out of sync
